title: Hebrews 7:1–10
context: The writer explains the mysterious Melchizedek, king of Salem and priest of God Most High, who met Abraham, blessed him, and received a tenth of the spoils. His name means king of righteousness, and his title means king of peace. Scripture records no genealogy for him, which makes him a fitting picture of the Son, who has a priesthood without end. Because the lesser is blessed by the greater, and Levi in a sense paid tithes through Abraham, Melchizedek’s priesthood is superior to Levi’s. The passage is common ground for both traditions.

verses.text: For this Melchizedek, king of Salem, priest of God Most High, who met Abraham returning from the slaughter of the kings and blessed him,
verses.arminianNotes: Melchizedek, king of Salem and priest of God Most High, met Abraham and blessed him. Arminian readers see God working through a priest outside Abraham’s line, which shows his concern for the nations.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see Melchizedek as a type of Christ, uniting the offices of king and priest.

verses.text: to whom also Abraham divided a tenth part of all (being first, by interpretation, “king of righteousness”, and then also “king of Salem”, which means “king of peace”,
verses.arminianNotes: Abraham gave him a tenth; his name means king of righteousness, and he is king of peace. Arminian readers see righteousness and peace joined in Christ for all who come to him.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see righteousness as the ground of peace, which Christ secures through his work (Romans 5:1).

verses.text: without father, without mother, without genealogy, having neither beginning of days nor end of life, but made like the Son of God), remains a priest continually.
verses.arminianNotes: Without father or mother or genealogy, having neither beginning of days nor end of life, resembling the Son of God, he remains a priest forever. Arminian readers see Scripture’s silence about his origins used as a picture of Christ’s eternal priesthood.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise read the verse typologically. A few have suggested Melchizedek was a pre-incarnate appearance of Christ, though most do not.

verses.text: Now consider how great this man was, to whom even Abraham the patriarch gave a tenth out of the best plunder.
verses.arminianNotes: See how great this man was, to whom Abraham gave a tenth. Arminian readers see the honor Abraham showed him as pointing to Christ’s greatness.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the patriarch acknowledging a greater priest, which foreshadows the superiority of Christ.

verses.text: They indeed of the sons of Levi who receive the priest’s office have a commandment to take tithes from the people according to the law, that is, of their brothers, though these have come out of the body of Abraham,
verses.arminianNotes: The Levitical priests receive tithes from their brothers under the law. Arminian readers see the old priesthood as limited to Israel.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the Levitical order as a temporary administration within God’s covenant.

verses.text: but he whose genealogy is not counted from them has accepted tithes from Abraham, and has blessed him who has the promises.
verses.arminianNotes: Melchizedek, not of their descent, received tithes from Abraham and blessed him who had the promises. Arminian readers see God’s blessing given beyond Israel’s formal structures.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the bearer of the promise blessed by a greater priest, which shows the superiority of Christ’s order.

verses.text: But without any dispute the lesser is blessed by the greater.
verses.arminianNotes: The lesser is blessed by the greater. Both traditions see the principle establishing Melchizedek’s superiority. Arminian readers apply it to Christ’s superiority over every earthly mediator.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see Christ, the greater priest, blessing his people.

verses.text: Here people who die receive tithes, but there one receives tithes of whom it is testified that he lives.
verses.arminianNotes: Mortal men receive tithes, but there it is testified that he lives. Arminian readers see a living priesthood that never ends.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see in this an image of Christ’s endless life, which makes his priesthood permanent.

verses.text: We can say that through Abraham even Levi, who receives tithes, has paid tithes,
verses.arminianNotes: Levi, who receives tithes, paid tithes through Abraham. Arminian readers see the old priesthood honoring the greater one.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see corporate representation: Levi acting in Abraham. Some connect this principle with federal headship in Adam and Christ.

verses.text: for he was yet in the body of his father when Melchizedek met him.
verses.arminianNotes: He was still in the loins of his ancestor when Melchizedek met him. Arminian readers see the writer’s argument from the unity of the family line.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see support for the idea that one person can act for those who come after, as in the doctrine of representation.
